title: Telling a grown-up when something feels wrong
keyIdea: Trusted grown-ups are people you know well who keep you safe, like a parent, a grandparent, your teacher or a nursery helper. A smile or sweets does not make someone a trusted grown-up. When you feel hurt, worried, scared, lost or uncomfortable, tell one of them. If you get lost in a shop, stay inside and ask a shop worker or a mum or dad with children. Your body belongs to you, so you can say no to a kiss, hug or tickle you do not want. A surprise is fine to keep for a little while, but a worry secret should be told. If the first grown-up is busy, keep telling until someone listens.
familyTip: Trace your child's hand on paper and write one trusted grown-up on each finger together. Stick it on the fridge. In a shop, point out who wears a staff badge or works at the till, and practise saying 'I'm lost. My name is…' together.

visual.caption: Should you tell a grown-up, or is it all OK? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: A secret makes me feel bad

lab.caption: Flagship lab: fill your helping hand, sort tell-or-OK moments, get help when lost in a shop, say no, sort secrets and keep telling.

kid: A trusted grown-up is someone you know well who keeps you safe. Mum, Dad, Gran, your teacher or your nursery helper can be one. A smile or sweets does not make a person safe.
Tell a trusted grown-up when you feel hurt, sad, scared or worried. Tell them when someone is unkind to you. You will not be in trouble for telling. They want to help.
Lost in a shop? Stop. Stay inside. Ask a shop worker at the till, or a mum or dad with children. Say your name.
Your body belongs to you. You can say no to a kiss, a hug or a tickle you do not want. A surprise is OK to keep for now. A worry secret is not. Tell it. If a grown-up is busy, tell another one.
adult: Ages 4 to 5, read it together. In the EYFS, Personal, Social and Emotional Development asks children to manage their own needs and to ask for help. The DfE's Relationships Education guidance ("Being safe") goes further. Children learn that each person's body belongs to them. They learn that some secrets should not be kept, and to keep asking for help until they are heard. The NSPCC's PANTS rules give the same messages at this age.

The lab builds a small safety plan. Your child names five trusted adults, one per finger. They learn which moments to tell: hurt, worried, scared, lost, or someone being unkind. If lost in a shop, they stay inside, go to a shop worker or a parent with children, and say their name. They practise saying no to touch they do not want. They sort happy surprises from worry secrets. Last, they learn to tell someone else if the first adult is busy.

Common mistakes: children often think telling is 'telling tales', or that they will be in trouble. When lost, they may run outside or hide. They may think anyone friendly is safe. They may keep a secret because a grown-up asked them to. Many give up after one busy adult. Adults slip too: making a child hug a relative, or brushing off a small worry, teaches that telling does not work. Thank your child every time they tell you something.

practice.prompt: Which one is a trusted grown-up?
choices: A person I do not know who smiles
practice.hint: Trusted grown-ups are people you know well.
practice.explain: Your teacher knows you and keeps you safe. A smile or sweets does not make a person someone you can trust.

practice.prompt: Ben is in a big shop with {n} aisles. He cannot see his dad. What should he do?
choices: Stay in the shop and ask a shop worker
practice.hint: Where will Dad look for Ben?
practice.explain: Ben should stay inside and ask a shop worker at the till. Dad will look for him in the shop. If he hides or goes outside, he is harder to find.

practice.prompt: Ava's cousin keeps tickling her. She has said stop {n} times. What can she do now?
practice.hint: Ava said stop. It did not stop. Who can help?
practice.explain: Ava should tell a grown-up. Her body belongs to her, and a grown-up can make the tickling stop.

practice.prompt: Which secret should you tell a grown-up about?
choices: Someone hurt me and said do not tell
A party for Dad on Sunday
practice.hint: Does the secret make you feel happy or bad?
practice.explain: A secret about being hurt is a worry secret, so tell it. A present or a party is a happy surprise that everyone finds out about soon.

pool.prompt: You fall over and hurt your knee at the park. What do you do?
choices: Wait and hope it goes away
pool.hint: Who can help make it better?
pool.explain: Tell a grown-up you know. You will not be in trouble, and they can clean your knee and help.

pool.prompt: Auntie wants a kiss. You do not want one. What can you do?
choices: Say no thank you and wave
pool.explain: You can say no thank you and give a wave or a high five. Auntie can still know you love her.

pool.prompt: You tell your teacher you are sad, but she is busy and does not hear. What next?
choices: Tell her again, or tell another grown-up
pool.hint: Do not give up. Who else is on your hand?
pool.explain: Keep telling. Ask her again when she is free, or tell another grown-up on your hand.

pool.prompt: Sam has {n} trusted grown-ups on his helping hand. A man he does not know asks him to come and see some puppies. What should Sam do?
choices: Say no and go to his grown-up
pool.explain: Sam should say no and go to his grown-up straight away, then tell them. Only go with someone your grown-up said yes to.

pool.prompt: Which one is a time to tell a grown-up?
choices: A big child keeps pushing me
I am playing with my friend
pool.hint: Which one feels bad or unsafe?
pool.explain: Being pushed again and again is a time to tell. A grown-up can stop it. The others are happy moments.

pool.prompt: You are lost in a shop. A shop worker asks your name. What do you say?
choices: My name and my grown-up's name
pool.hint: What helps the shop worker find your grown-up?
pool.explain: Say your name and your grown-up's name. Then the shop worker can call for them.

pool.prompt: It is {n} days to Dad's birthday. You and Mum have a present for him. Is it OK to keep it secret?
choices: Yes, it is a happy surprise
pool.hint: Is it a happy surprise or a worry?
pool.explain: It is a happy surprise, so keep it until his birthday. Then everyone knows. A secret that makes you feel bad should be told.

pool.prompt: Why do we tell a grown-up when something feels wrong?
choices: So they can help keep us safe
pool.explain: Telling helps a grown-up keep you safe. It is never naughty to tell when you feel hurt, worried or scared.
